source.title: Before the First Token: Scale-Dependent Emergence of Hallucination Signals in Autoregressive Language Models
source.authors: Dip Roy; Rajiv Misra; Sanjay Kumar Singh; A. Roy

record.file_problem: The body is a complete paper, but its title (“Detection Without Correction: A Robust Asymmetry in ActivationBased Hallucination Probing”) does not match the supplied title (“Before the First Token: Scale-Dependent Emergence of Hallucination Signals in Autoregressive Language Models”).
record.tranche_reason: It reports TriviaQA exact-match accuracy across models of different sizes, bearing on downstream performance versus scale (V6), but does not measure held-out pretraining loss or reproduce the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The study reports no held-out cross-entropy sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute, and no compute-optimal allocation. Its probe AUC, steering, and temporal-position results concern hallucination detection or correction, not the loss-scaling versions; they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: A hallucination-probing paper that incidentally reports TriviaQA exact-match accuracy for seven pretrained models (117M–7B), including a four-point Pythia series and a two-point GPT-2 series. This bears weakly on V6, whether downstream accuracy improves with scale, in a setting not designed for it. No curve is fitted and there is no link to loss. Nothing bears on V1–V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that probe-direction steering corrects no hallucinations in any of the 7 models. They find output-confidence baselines beat probes on detection AUC above 410M parameters. They argue the probes' value is pre-generation (position-0) flagging, significant in only two models. They make no claim about scaling laws or downstream accuracy scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Measures TriviaQA exact-match accuracy across existing models of different sizes rather than held-out pretraining loss across controlled parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The models vary in architecture, training corpus, and post-training condition; the paper notes these differences are confounded in cross-model comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Probe detection AUC for hallucination depends on model scale. Sub-400M models are near chance and a position-0 signal appears in some models above about 1B, but not in Pythia-6.9B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear-probe detectability of hallucination signals emerges with model scale, but not monotonically.

record.code_released: not stated; code and experimental materials are available on request.
record.problems: For the downstream-accuracy comparison, the models are not a controlled size series and differ in architecture, training data, and post-training. The reported accuracy values have no uncertainty estimates, and the study does not fit or validate a predictive scaling curve.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for probe AUC, activation steering, or temporal-position contrasts: those measure hallucination detection/correction behavior, not a versioned loss-scaling outcome or downstream task accuracy.

untested.parts: No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No loss comparison across shapes at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No fitted downstream scaling relation, no prediction of larger models, and accuracy is not related to pretraining loss.

missing.what: Per-model accuracy on the auxiliary Simple Facts (n=32) and Biography (n=20) tasks. Shown only in a heatmap; authors draw no conclusions from it.

record.verdict_notes: The file's title mismatch noted by the reader is real but harmless: the body is a complete paper. The V6 evidence is incidental: accuracy is reported as a capability/class-balance check, with only 4 Pythia points and 2 GPT-2 points and no uncertainty on accuracy. Weight it lightly. Pythia is a controlled suite (same data and order), so the within-Pythia trend is the cleanest part. There is an internal inconsistency: '61%' in the text vs 64.1% in Table 2 for Qwen2.5-7B.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No comparison of language-model loss across architectures at fixed parameter count.
No loss-scaling tests in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Reports TriviaQA exact-match accuracy across differently sized models, but does not fit a predictive scaling relation or relate accuracy to pretraining loss.
No fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal split are compared across setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated exact-match accuracy across differently sized models on TriviaQA.
rows.note: One point in a cross-model size comparison; no fitted downstream scaling curve is reported.
rows.check: Single point. Read it with R5 as the GPT-2 family pair: 13.2% at 117M rises to 29.3% at 1.5B. Accuracy has no uncertainty (the record's 'uncertainty_reported: y' covers AUC only).

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated exact-match accuracy across differently sized models on TriviaQA.
rows.note: One point in a cross-model size comparison; the value is below GPT-2 Small despite the slightly larger parameter count.
rows.check: Lowest point of a monotone Pythia series (9.6, 21.0, 33.3, 43.8%). State is meaningful only as part of R2–R4 and R6.

rows.subject: GPT-2 XL
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated exact-match accuracy across differently sized models on TriviaQA.
rows.note: Accuracy is below that of the smaller Pythia-1.4B model; models differ in architecture and training data.
rows.check: Higher than GPT-2 Small within its family. Across families it is below the smaller Pythia-1.4B (29.3% vs 33.3%).

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated exact-match accuracy across differently sized models on TriviaQA.
rows.note: One point in a cross-model size comparison; it differs in architecture, training corpus, and post-training from the other models.
rows.check: The only Qwen model, instruction-tuned with RLHF, with a different corpus. There is no within-family size comparison. The text also says the largest model reaches '61% accuracy', which conflicts with 64.1% in Table 2.

relationships.condition: Within family: Pythia 160M–6.9B and GPT-2 117M–1.5B, TriviaQA exact match, greedy decoding
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises monotonically with size within each family: Pythia 9.6→21.0→33.3→43.8% and GPT-2 13.2→29.3%. The trend is not fitted (R1–R6).
relationships.display_finding: Pythia accuracy increased 9.6%→21.0%→33.3%→43.8% and GPT-2 accuracy increased 13.2%→29.3%, without a fitted scaling relation.

relationships.reason: Parameter count alone does not order accuracy across families. GPT-2 XL (1.5B) scores 29.3% vs Pythia-1.4B's 33.3%, and GPT-2 Small beats Pythia-160M (R1, R2, R4, R5).
relationships.display_finding: GPT-2 XL at 1.5B scored 29.3% versus Pythia-1.4B's 33.3%, while GPT-2 Small beat Pythia-160M.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
